strengths: Novel finite-sample theoretical analysis of iterative self-improvement that rigorously captures practical phenomena (feedback loops, saturation, budget constraints) missed by asymptotic analysis
Explicit formalization of the virtuous cycle where better models accept more data per iteration, explaining both sustained improvement and eventual saturation
Rigorous technical framework (Theorems 4.1, 5.2; Corollary 4.4) using sound empirical process theory with correct proofs throughout appendix
Quantifiable conditions with practical interpretation (moderate task difficulty regimes, phase transitions, optimal curriculum parameters) that guide practitioner understanding
Strong empirical validation within scope: experiments directly confirm theoretical predictions on synthetic tasks (Figures 3-4 match theoretical phase-space predictions precisely)
Task-centric approach integrating model initialization quality with downstream difficulty, providing timely theoretical contribution to curriculum learning for self-improvement
Careful treatment of assumptions with justifications and honest limitations discussion; comprehensive appendix enables reproducibility
weaknesses: Experimental validation limited to synthetic graph shortest-path tasks; no experiments on real reasoning benchmarks (MATH, Lean, code) limits confidence that insights transfer to stated practical motivation despite theoretical rigor

Key assumptions (Assumption 4.3 reward-acceptance coupling, Assumption 5.1 power-law task difficulty) lack empirical validation on real tasks; unclear if c and γ parameters are realistic or how sensitive results are to violations

Loose bounds with unclear tightness: √(log|Π|/n) dependence is standard but no lower bounds provided; conditions sufficient but potentially not necessary; improvement condition N < 0 analytically opaque (Definition A.2)

Theory-practice gaps unaddressed: no guidance on setting reward threshold τ; Figure 3(c) shows empirishing returns for m contradicting monotonic improvement predictions; modern soft-filtering strategies not captured

Limited practical impact: Figure 4(b) shows modest 2-5% Pass@1 improvements in specific budget regimes only; practitioners already use easy-to-hard curricula, so theory explains but doesn't suggest novel strategies

Presentation issues: feasibility conditions {M_i < 0} relegated to appendix despite centrality to main results; improvement condition N < 0 too complex for practitioners; Figures 1-2 hard to interpret
Binary reward assumption restrictive; real reasoning systems use nuanced reward signals not captured by s(q,a)∈{0,1}; extension to continuous rewards unclear
